title: His Missing Hand Stayed Clenched for 10 Years, Until a Mirror Box Opened It
description:
Ten years after losing his left arm in an accident, amputee Philip Martinez still felt his missing phantom fist frozen in an agonizing cramp that nerve surgery could never reach (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran 1995, Nature; Ramachandran 1998, Brain). At UC San Diego, behavioral neurologist V. S. Ramachandran first mapped face-to-phantom-hand remapping along primary somatosensory cortex with a simple cotton swab, then stood a $10 glass mirror upright inside an open cardboard box—letting 6 of 10 tested upper-limb amputees watch a reflected twin hand stretch wide open and feel frozen phantom spasms unclench.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Ramachandran VS (1998) The perception of phantom limbs. The D. O. Hebb lecture. Brain 121(9): 1603-1630. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/121.9.1603
- Ramachandran VS, Rogers-Ramachandran D, Cobb S (1995) Touching the phantom limb. Nature 377: 489-490. https://doi.org/10.1038/377489a0
